title: A river without a crossing
text: Look at the two towers in front of you. Now, imagine this stretch of river without them. In eighteen seventy-six, London was calling for another crossing here. But tall ships needed to reach the warehouses upstream. How could a road cross the Thames without closing the river? Keep that question in mind.

title: A bridge takes shape
text: Watch the bridge take shape. Construction began in eighteen eighty-six, and lasted eight years. First, foundations and piers. Then, a great steel skeleton rose above the water. Look closely: the towers may look like a castle, but their stone exterior covers a steel framework. The two high walkways connect them. Below, the roadway has a gap. This is where the clever part happens.

title: Make way for the river
text: Follow the road between the towers. Watch its two halves rise. Each is called a bascule, a word meaning seesaw. Balanced around a pivot, the roadway swings upward to clear a path for tall ships. The bridge opened in June, eighteen ninety-four. Imagine standing here as a ship slipped through, with the road suspended above the water. A crossing for London. A passage for the river.

title: Look again
text: Now, watch how the bridge changes. In nineteen seventy-six, electric pumps replaced the steam-powered system. The bridge still used hydraulics, but its source of power changed. A year later, its older chocolate brown paint gave way to red, white and blue for the Queen's Silver Jubilee. Look back at the real bridge. The colours and machinery have changed. The need to keep the river open has not.
